labs.objective: Read the value of app.config['FLAG'] and submit it. The flag is loaded into Flask config at startup from /flag.txt (readable only by the flask process).
labs.flag_hint: The Flask app loads /flag.txt into config['FLAG'] at boot. Solve by making the vulnerable template render that value into the HTTP response, then paste the string into POST /solve which does a constant-time compare against the file and returns {"solved": true, "flag": "..."} on match.
labs.inspired_by: Classic PortSwigger Academy Lab 'Basic server-side template injection' (Jinja2 variant) — abstracted with a fresh greeting-card story.

labs.title: Twig Debug Toolbar Left On
labs.description: A Symfony 6.4 blog left twig.debug=true in prod and renders user 'signature' fields through {{ signature|raw }}. Users inject {{ 7*7 }}, then {{ dump(_context) }} via the debug filter to dump every variable in scope — including a hidden $adminInviteToken variable set by a controller for a nearby admin panel. The lab teaches how debug mode alone turns a low-severity template render into full context exfiltration before any RCE.
labs.objective: Exfiltrate the $adminInviteToken variable that only exists in the template render context (never sent to the client) and POST it to /admin/redeem to receive the flag.
labs.flag_hint: Endpoint POST /admin/redeem accepts {token: '...'}; if it matches the per-container random token (regenerated on boot, stored only in Symfony service container), it returns the flag from /flag.txt in the JSON body.
skills_taught: abuse of dump()/_context in debug mode
understanding template scope vs response body
why twig.debug must be false in prod
labs.inspired_by: Recurring bug-bounty class of findings where Symfony apps ship with APP_ENV=dev in prod; abstracted from multiple HackerOne reports on French e-commerce sites.

labs.title: ERB in the Rails 'Email Preview' Panel
labs.description: An internal marketing tool lets logged-in users preview an email by pasting an ERB snippet into a textarea; the server calls ERB.new(params[:body]).result(binding) so it can substitute {{first_name}}. The intent was Liquid-style, but the dev reached for ERB by accident. Users learn ERB syntax <%= 7*7 %>, then <%= `id` %>, then <%= File.read('/flag.txt') %>. Rails 7.1, Ruby 3.3.
labs.objective: Read /flag.txt from inside the container and submit its contents.
labs.flag_hint: A file exists at /flag.txt readable by the rails user (mode 0640, owner rails:rails). Submit the string to POST /solve which does a constant-time compare against the file's bytes.
skills_taught: identifying template engines from framework hints
labs.inspired_by: Real Rails-shop finding pattern seen in multiple 2023–2024 HackerOne 'email designer' reports.

labs.title: AngularJS 1.4 Client-Side Template Injection
labs.description: A single-page comment widget still runs AngularJS 1.4 (frozen since a vendor lock-in). The site renders comment bodies inside an <div ng-app> block without sanitization. Users learn CSTI by injecting {{constructor.constructor('alert(1)')()}} and understand why the AngularJS scope acts as an eval sandbox waiting to be escaped. Delivered as a static Nginx site — no backend needed — to isolate the CSTI concept.
labs.objective: Trigger an XSS that reads document.cookie and POSTs it (with fetch) to http://oob:9000/exfil. The 'oob' container listens on 9000 and issues the flag once a request with a valid session cookie arrives.
labs.flag_hint: A second container named 'oob' on the compose network listens on port 9000 at /exfil?cookie=. When it receives a request containing the string 'PHPSESSID=' followed by any hex, it writes the flag to a shared volume file /solve/flag.txt and returns it in the response body.
labs.inspired_by: Mario Heiderich's original AngularJS sandbox-escape research; the 1.4.x scope escape ladder documented on PortSwigger.

labs.title: Handlebars 'Echo Bot' — Just Print the Input
labs.description: A tiny Express + Handlebars echo service compiles the user's message as a template ('so you can use {{name}}!') and renders it with the request context. Users learn Handlebars fingerprinting via {{7*7}} returning '49' vs. Handlebars' actual behavior of returning '' (Handlebars does NOT evaluate arithmetic — a great teaching moment), then use {{#with 'constructor'}} tricks to walk the prototype and leak the FLAG variable placed in the render context.
labs.objective: Read the value of context.FLAG (set from process.env.FLAG at boot) and print it into the response.
labs.flag_hint: process.env.FLAG is loaded from /flag.txt on container start and passed only into the template render context — never sent as JSON. Solve by making the compiled template output the flag, then paste it to POST /solve for constant-time verification.
skills_taught: difference between compile-time and runtime template context
reading env-only secrets via template scope
labs.inspired_by: Common intro CSTI/SSTI mistake in chat-bot MVPs seen in 2023–2024 startup bug bounties.

labs.title: Jinja2 — From {{config}} to Full RCE
labs.description: A Flask feedback form filters out the strings 'os', 'popen', 'system', and 'import' but does not filter dunder attributes, __class__, __mro__, __subclasses__, or the Jinja2 request object. Users walk the classic ladder: {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }} → find subprocess.Popen → invoke Popen(['cat','/flag.txt'], stdout=-1).communicate()[0]. The lab teaches the anatomy of the Python object graph and why blocking string substrings is not enough.
labs.objective: Execute an OS command that reads /flag.txt (owner root, mode 0644, but not readable by the app user — you need to escalate via the exact Popen invocation the lab provides no shortcut for).
labs.flag_hint: /flag.txt is world-readable; the app user just doesn't have a shell. Solve = make Popen return the flag bytes into the response. Verify at POST /solve.
skills_taught: locating subprocess.Popen in the class list
why substring filters fail against attribute chains
labs.inspired_by: PayloadsAllTheThings SSTI cheatsheet — the canonical Jinja2 mro ladder every pentester learns.

labs.title: Twig — sort() + call_user_func + system()
labs.description: A Symfony 6.4 email builder renders subject lines with a raw Twig context and allows filters. The blacklist strips 'exec' and 'passthru' but permits |map, |filter, |sort, and |reduce. Users chain {{ ['id']|filter('system') }} — Twig applies system() as the callback to each element, executing it. Then they escalate to cat /flag.txt. Teaches how Twig's higher-order filter functions become arbitrary function invokers when user input reaches the callback slot.
labs.objective: Execute `cat /flag.txt` via a Twig filter callback and return the output in the rendered subject line preview.
labs.flag_hint: GET /solve verifies via checker script — the rendered HTML must contain the exact 32-hex flag string generated at container boot and written to /flag.txt (mode 0644).
skills_taught: bypassing deny-lists that miss filter chains
labs.inspired_by: Twig sort()/filter() callback abuse popularized by ambionics/security research (2021) and reused in multiple 2023 HackerOne reports.

labs.title: Freemarker `new()` + Execute — Struts-style RCE
labs.description: A Spring MVC ticket system uses Freemarker to render user-supplied issue descriptions with allow_html=true and default sandbox settings (which are permissive). Users invoke <#assign ex='freemarker.template.utility.Execute'?new()>${ex('id')} — the ?new() built-in instantiates Java classes if the TemplateClassResolver allows it (default in older Freemarker or misconfigured 2.3.31+). Teaches the Freemarker exploitation primitive that powered years of Struts and Confluence exploits.
labs.objective: Execute `id` via freemarker.template.utility.Execute and capture the output in the HTTP response, then submit uid+gid string to /solve.
labs.flag_hint: The checker /solve runs a subprocess `id` inside the container itself and compares your submission against its output — proving your RCE ran in-container. On match, returns /flag.txt.
skills_taught: why 'sandboxed' Freemarker isn't sandboxed by default
labs.inspired_by: Freemarker ?new() Execute pattern behind Apache OFBiz and many pre-2020 Struts findings; still resurfacing in Confluence-adjacent products in 2023.

labs.title: Velocity — RuntimeSingleton + Runtime.exec()
labs.description: A Confluence-alike wiki uses Apache Velocity 1.7 to render user 'macros' inside page templates. Users inject #set($rt=$Class.forName('java.lang.Runtime').getRuntime()) followed by $rt.exec('id'). Because the app registered $Class into the Velocity context (a real 2019–2022 anti-pattern from tutorials), full RCE follows. Users must also handle Velocity's quirky output (Process object toString) by using .getInputStream() + InputStreamReader.
labs.objective: Execute a shell command in the container and read /flag.txt (mode 0640, owner appuser:appuser, app runs as appuser so it IS readable — just needs command execution).
labs.flag_hint: Solve = paste the /flag.txt contents into POST /solve. The lab README shows a Runtime.exec pipeline for reading files. Constant-time compare against file bytes.
skills_taught: consuming Process stdout in Velocity via InputStreamReader
why passing $Class into template context is fatal
labs.inspired_by: Velocity RCE pattern documented across Apache Solr, OFBiz, and Confluence — the $Class-in-context anti-pattern from Java tutorials.

labs.title: Thymeleaf Preprocessor `__${...}__` to SpEL RCE
labs.description: A Spring Boot 3.3 profile page renders th:text with a partial user-controlled fragment name. The dev used the double-underscore preprocessor to build fragment paths dynamically: th:fragment="__${param.frag}__". Preprocessors run SpEL BEFORE any output escaping, giving RCE via T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec('id'). Users learn the difference between Thymeleaf expression contexts (${}, *{}, @{}, ~{}) and how preprocessor semantics defeat escaping.
labs.objective: Execute `cat /flag.txt` via SpEL through the Thymeleaf preprocessor and reflect the result on the page.
labs.flag_hint: checker.sh runs inside the container comparing the response body against /flag.txt bytes (32 hex chars). Endpoint GET /solve triggers it against the last-rendered HTML for your session.
skills_taught: SpEL T() type reference for Runtime
labs.inspired_by: Aleksei Tiurin's Thymeleaf research (Acunetix, 2019) — still findings in 2024 pentests of internal Spring apps.

labs.title: Handlebars — require() via Constructor Walk
labs.description: A Node.js Express 4 report-generator lets users write subject-line templates in Handlebars. Users escape via {{#with 'constructor'}} → walk to the Function constructor via prototype pollution of a helper, then Function('return process')().mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id'). This teaches the classic Node CSTI-to-RCE walk without prototype pollution — pure template abuse. Comparison lab to Node.js template CVEs.
labs.objective: Execute execSync('cat /flag.txt') via Handlebars and echo the output into the report subject.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve accepts the flag string; constant-time compare against /flag.txt (32 hex, owner node:node, mode 0640).
skills_taught: why Handlebars 'strict' mode still exposes primitives
labs.inspired_by: Mahmoud Gamal's Handlebars SSTI research (2019) and its 2023 revival in serverless template-render services.

labs.title: Nunjucks — range() Object Prototype to RCE
labs.description: A Node.js dashboard uses Nunjucks (Mozilla's Jinja2 port) to render user-defined widget titles. Users inject {{ range.constructor("return global.process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id')")() }} — Nunjucks exposes range as a JS Array whose .constructor is Array, whose .constructor... chain leads to Function. Teaches the Nunjucks-specific primitive and why Jinja2 lore ports 90% cleanly.
labs.objective: Read /flag.txt via child_process.execSync and echo the result in the widget title preview.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve; constant-time compare against /flag.txt (owner node:node).
skills_taught: how JS-side globals leak into template scope
labs.inspired_by: James Kettle's Nunjucks research (SSTI whitepaper, 2015) — the range object trick, still hitting in 2024 dashboards.

labs.title: EJS — outputFunctionName Injection to RCE
labs.description: An Express 4 app passes user-controlled JSON straight into res.render('view', body). If body contains {settings: {view options: {outputFunctionName: '...'}}} or the older {outputFunctionName: 'x;code;x'} pattern, an attacker injects arbitrary JS into the compiled template body. Users exploit CVE-2022-29078-style EJS RCE end-to-end and understand why res.render must never receive attacker-controlled option keys.
labs.objective: Execute child_process.execSync('cat /flag.txt') via the EJS outputFunctionName option and return the flag in the response.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve, constant-time compare against /flag.txt (32 hex).
skills_taught: why merging user JSON into render options is dangerous
labs.inspired_by: CVE-2022-29078 (EJS outputFunctionName RCE).

labs.title: Pug/Jade — Runtime Compile of Attacker Templates
labs.description: A CMS lets marketing users write email templates in Pug. The backend calls pug.compile(userSource)() every send. Pug is a full JS DSL — users escape via - const x = global.process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id'); or by using `#{...}` interpolation with Function('return process'). Teaches that ANY template engine that compiles arbitrary source at runtime is equivalent to eval().
labs.objective: Execute a shell command reading /flag.txt inside the container.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve; constant-time compare against /flag.txt.
skills_taught: Node process access from Pug scope
labs.inspired_by: Common finding in CMS/email-builder pentests 2022–2024; abstracted from multiple Bugcrowd disclosures.

labs.title: Liquid — Custom Drop Class Method Discovery
labs.description: A merchant storefront uses Ruby Liquid with a custom UserDrop class that inadvertently exposes .system_call via method_missing. Users enumerate the Drop's method surface via {{ user | inspect }}, discover the leaky method, and chain {{ user.system_call: 'cat /flag.txt' }} for RCE. Teaches how the 'safe' Liquid model breaks when custom Drops don't override method_missing.
labs.objective: Invoke the leaked method and print /flag.txt contents to the storefront page.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve, constant-time compare against /flag.txt (mode 0644, owner ruby:ruby).
skills_taught: why 'safe' template engines depend on host-object hygiene
labs.inspired_by: Shopify's own Bug Bounty program disclosures about Drop method_missing footguns (2022–2023).

labs.title: Mustache — Lambda Section Rendering Confusion
labs.description: A Go microservice renders user-controlled Mustache templates. The dev exposed a helper 'shell' lambda for internal admin templates but forgot to strip it from user context. Users invoke {{#shell}}cat /flag.txt{{/shell}} — the lambda receives the section body and shell-executes it. Teaches how 'logic-less' Mustache becomes dangerous when hosts add lambda helpers.
labs.objective: Read /flag.txt via the exposed shell lambda.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve, constant-time compare against /flag.txt (owner go:go).
skills_taught: differentiating user vs. admin template contexts
labs.inspired_by: Recurring 'admin lambda leaked to user template' pattern in Go microservices; abstracted from Gitea-adjacent finding classes.

labs.title: Smarty — {math} + Static Method Call Bypass
labs.description: A PHP CMS uses Smarty 4.5 with SecurityPolicy set to disable {php} and {literal}. Users can still exploit via {math equation='sqrt(x)' x=self::getStreamContents(1)} tricks and static method calls the security policy forgot to blacklist. Users must enumerate the allowed function list, find one that reaches file_get_contents indirectly, and read /flag.txt. Teaches the failure modes of allow-list-based template security.
labs.objective: Read /flag.txt via a chain that stays inside the SecurityPolicy allow-list.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve; constant-time compare against /flag.txt (mode 0640, owner www-data:www-data).
labs.inspired_by: Smarty {math} static-method finding chain published in 2023 by SonarSource researchers.

labs.title: Jinja2 — Bypass a 30-token Blacklist
labs.description: A Flask app blacklists: {{, }}, {%, %}, __, class, mro, subclasses, config, request, self, application, popen, system, exec, import, subprocess, os, sh, bash, eval, compile, getattr, globals, builtins, lipsum, cycler, joiner, namespace, and quotes. Users must chain: {%if... use of |attr(request.args.a) to fetch dunder attributes, use of |attr('\x5f\x5fclass\x5f\x5f'), request via url_for.__globals__, and the lipsum.__globals__ alternative when lipsum isn't blocked. This is the definitive filter-bypass ladder lab.
labs.objective: Execute a shell command and read /flag.txt despite the aggressive blacklist.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve; the checker also verifies your payload does not literally contain any blacklisted token (the platform runs the same regex on your submission), forcing you to bypass rather than smuggle.
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger Academy 'SSTI in an unknown context with a documented exploit' + community CTF Jinja2 bypass challenges (HTB, picoCTF).

labs.title: Twig SandboxExtension — Escape via ArrayAccess
labs.description: A Symfony app renders user templates inside a strict Twig SandboxExtension (only 'upper', 'lower', 'length' filters; only Post entity allowed). Users must escape by abusing an ArrayAccess object leaked into context whose offsetGet triggers Doctrine hydration that instantiates a controllable class — reaching a gadget chain. The lab reproduces the Twig SandboxExtension bypass class documented by ambionics. Requires patience and object-graph reasoning.
labs.objective: Escape the sandbox and read /flag.txt.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve; constant-time compare against /flag.txt.
skills_taught: reading Twig source to find sandbox holes
labs.inspired_by: ambionics security research on Twig SandboxExtension bypasses (2021–2022) and CVE-2023-46734 lineage.

labs.title: AngularJS 1.6 — CSTI After Sandbox Was Removed
labs.description: The AngularJS team removed the expression sandbox in 1.6 because 'it wasn't a security feature'. This lab embeds AngularJS 1.6.10 in a chat widget where message bodies flow into an ng-bind-html-unsafe-equivalent block. Users craft {{constructor.constructor('return globalThis')().fetch(...)}} payloads to exfiltrate a session cookie belonging to an admin user simulated by a headless-Chromium bot that visits every posted message. Teaches CSP-lite bypass in the sandbox-removed era.
labs.objective: Steal the admin bot's session cookie (containing a bearer token) and POST it to http://oob:9000/exfil to receive the flag.
labs.flag_hint: A headless-Chromium bot (bundled container 'bot') visits every posted message once with an admin cookie set. Deliver the cookie to the OOB listener on port 9000; on receipt it writes /solve/flag.txt into a shared volume.
skills_taught: orchestrating an admin-visits-you flow with a bot
CSTI vs traditional stored XSS distinction
labs.inspired_by: AngularJS security disclosures around 1.6 release notes (2016) and their long tail in 2022–2024 legacy audits.

labs.title: Vue 2 — v-html + Mustache in Same Node
labs.description: A Vue 2.7 dashboard renders user comments with :inner-html.prop bound to a computed that runs Vue.compile on the raw comment ('for markdown-lite support'). Users craft templates with <template v-for> and inline expressions that reach the Vue prototype, then via _self.$root walk to a globally exposed axios instance to make same-origin requests as the admin user. Ends in fetching /admin/api/flag via CSRF-token-included in the same-origin fetch.
labs.objective: As the admin bot, fetch /admin/api/flag (which requires a same-origin CSRF token from the DOM) and exfiltrate the returned flag to http://oob:9000/exfil.
labs.flag_hint: Bot container ('bot') logs in as admin and views each new comment. On successful exfil to :9000, the OOB listener writes the flag to /solve/flag.txt.
labs.inspired_by: Recurrent 2023–2024 finding class in Vue 2 legacy dashboards migrating to Vue 3.

labs.title: wkhtmltopdf — HTML-to-PDF SSTI + Local File Read
labs.description: An invoice generator renders a Jinja2 HTML template into PDF via wkhtmltopdf with --enable-local-file-access. Users first do standard Jinja2 SSTI to inject <iframe src='file:///flag.txt'> or an <object> tag, then retrieve the rendered PDF to read the file's contents from the resulting PDF. This teaches that SSTI in a PDF pipeline yields file-read even when the Python side is well-sandboxed, thanks to the QtWebKit renderer.
labs.objective: Read /flag.txt via file:// scheme leaked into the generated PDF, then submit the extracted string.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve with the exact flag string; constant-time compare against /flag.txt (owner root, mode 0644 — readable to wkhtmltopdf).
skills_taught: file:// scheme in <iframe>/<object> for PDF exfil
PDF text extraction as the last mile
labs.inspired_by: Multiple 2020–2023 HackerOne wkhtmltopdf SSRF/LFI reports; abstracted from the invoice-generator finding archetype.

labs.title: WeasyPrint — SSTI to SSRF to Cloud Metadata (Chain)
labs.description: A SaaS PDF exporter uses Jinja2 to render templates then WeasyPrint to convert. Jinja2 has a strict sandbox — but users inject a WeasyPrint-parsed which the PDF renderer fetches server-side. Users must then extract the AWS temporary credentials from the resulting PDF's embedded image bytes (base64-encoded response body), sign an STS GetCallerIdentity call, and use it to fetch /flag from an S3 object.
labs.objective: Chain: (1) SSTI-render an HTML that WeasyPrint fetches from 169.254.169.254; (2) extract AWS temp creds from the PDF; (3) call the mock STS/S3 endpoint at http://cloud:5000 to sign a request for s3://flag-bucket/flag.txt; (4) submit the flag.
labs.flag_hint: Mock cloud metadata + STS/S3 services run in a 'cloud' compose container. The 'cloud' container returns the flag when it sees a correctly SigV4-signed GET for the object using the app-role temp creds it minted for this attempt.
skills_taught: chaining template render → SSRF → cloud creds
mock IMDS + STS for realistic cloud practice
labs.inspired_by: The class of 2022–2023 HackerOne findings on PDF-generation SaaS that chain HTML-render SSRF into AWS IMDS credential theft.

labs.title: Rails ActionMailer — ERB SSTI via Preview Interceptor
labs.description: A Rails 7.1 SaaS lets users author mail 'preview snippets' stored as ERB. An admin preview endpoint renders them via ActionMailer::Preview. Users get RCE by classical ERB, but the twist: the flag is not in a file — it's a value inside Rails.application.credentials.dig(:flag). Users must walk Rails internals from within the mail preview render context to reach the credentials object. Teaches internal-framework object navigation.
labs.objective: Read Rails.application.credentials.dig(:flag) via ERB executed inside the ActionMailer preview.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve, constant-time compare against the credentials value (which the app also writes to a checker-only file /solve/flag.txt at boot for the verifier to compare).
skills_taught: reaching framework singletons from render scope
ERB in mail templates vs web templates
labs.inspired_by: Recurring bug-bounty finding class on Rails SaaS admin-mail preview interfaces (2023–2024).

labs.title: Spring Boot Actuator + SpEL — Heapdump-to-Secret to Template RCE
labs.description: A four-step elite chain: (1) discover /actuator/heapdump exposed (misconfigured); (2) mine the heapdump for a signing key belonging to a JWT that unlocks an admin template-editor endpoint; (3) authenticate to /admin/templates and submit a Thymeleaf snippet containing SpEL __${T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec('cat /flag.txt')}__; (4) chain the output into a callback response. This is the canonical modern Spring exploit chain, condensed.
labs.objective: Complete the four-step chain and read /flag.txt inside the container.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve, constant-time compare against /flag.txt (owner spring:spring, mode 0640). checker.sh also validates the heapdump was actually downloaded (audit log inspection).
skills_taught: heap-dump analysis with jhat/Eclipse MAT (or grep)
JWT forgery with recovered signing keys
Thymeleaf preprocessor + SpEL in admin template editors
labs.inspired_by: CVE-2022-22963 (Spring Cloud Function SpEL) + generalized Actuator-heapdump exposure findings on HackerOne 2022–2024.

labs.title: OGNL/Freemarker RCE — Confluence-CVE-2022-26134-style
labs.description: A pared-down Java web app reproduces the essence of CVE-2022-26134: a URL path element is evaluated as an OGNL expression by a naive JSP tag. Users craft ${(#a=@org.apache.commons.io.IOUtils@toString(@java.lang.Runtime@getRuntime().exec('cat /flag.txt').getInputStream()))}. The lab does NOT redistribute Confluence code — it's a 200-line Java servlet demonstrating the same primitive. Users must understand OGNL's #context, @Class@method syntax, and how to smuggle payloads in URL path segments.
labs.objective: Execute cat /flag.txt via OGNL smuggled in a URL path segment.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve, constant-time compare against /flag.txt (owner tomcat:tomcat, mode 0640).
skills_taught: URL path segment as expression vector
abstracting a real CVE into minimal repro
labs.inspired_by: CVE-2022-26134 (Atlassian Confluence OGNL RCE) — abstracted; no proprietary code included.

labs.title: Jinja2 — Blind SSTI with DNS/HTTP OOB
labs.description: The vulnerable app renders a Jinja2 template but never echoes the result — output goes only to a background PDF worker whose output the user cannot see. Users must exploit blindly: no output feedback at all. They exfiltrate via DNS lookups (using socket in a walked module) or HTTP callbacks to an OOB container on port 9000. The lab teaches boolean-based SSTI oracles, timing-based confirmation with time.sleep, and byte-by-byte exfil design.
labs.objective: Read /flag.txt and exfiltrate the 32-hex flag byte-by-byte to the OOB listener at http://oob:9000/exfil?byte=XX&pos=N (a helper Python script is provided).
labs.flag_hint: OOB listener assembles the bytes; when a complete 32-char valid flag arrives, it writes /solve/flag.txt to a shared volume and returns the flag when POST /solve is called.
skills_taught: socket/urllib walked from Python object graph
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger's blind SSTI academy content + James Kettle's OOB exploitation talks; 2023 GitLab HackerOne blind-SSTI report class.

labs.title: Gift Card Double Redeem
labs.description: A small e-commerce site lets logged-in users redeem $50 promo gift cards. The redemption endpoint reads the card row, checks status='unused', credits the wallet, then writes status='used' in three separate SQL statements with no row lock and no unique constraint on (card_id, wallet_id). Two near-simultaneous requests both pass the 'unused' check and both credit the wallet. This lab is the classic on-ramp to time-of-check/time-of-use thinking: the student sees a two-line curl pipeline turn $50 into $150 and understands why 'if not used' has to be an atomic UPDATE ... WHERE status='unused' RETURNING id.
labs.objective: Redeem the single-use gift card GC-STARTER-50 three times against your wallet so that /api/wallet/me shows balance >= 150. When balance crosses the threshold, POST /api/solve returns /flag.txt.
labs.flag_hint: HTTP endpoint POST /api/solve reads /flag.txt (mounted read-only into the container at /flag.txt) and returns it only if wallet.balance_cents >= 15000 AND wallet.owner_id == authenticated user. The check is a single SELECT so students cannot bypass it, only satisfy it.
skills_taught: why atomic UPDATE RETURNING beats SELECT-then-UPDATE
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger Web Security Academy 'Limit overrun race conditions' apprentice lab and the 2019 Starbucks gift card race writeup by Egor Homakov / sam-eb (abstracted; no proprietary code)

labs.title: Hidden Price Field Tamper
labs.description: A classic PHP checkout ships the item price as a hidden form input rendered from the product page and trusts it on POST /checkout. Intercepting the request in Burp and changing price=99900 to price=1 sells the $999 Pro License for one cent. There is no race and no concurrency; the whole lab teaches the student to distrust anything round-tripped through the client and to grep server code for req.body.price. A second premium item is priced with a nested JSON structure ({"pricing":{"final":{"cents":...}}}) to make sure the student learns to change nested fields too.
labs.objective: Purchase the Pro License (SKU=pro-license, list price $999) for total_cents <= 100 and load /orders/{id}/receipt. The receipt page renders the flag when the order is 'paid' AND item_sku='pro-license' AND total_cents <= 100.
labs.flag_hint: The receipt template at /orders/{id}/receipt reads /flag from disk (file mounted at /flag, mode 0444) and renders it in a <div id='flag'> only when the SQL predicate above holds. No separate /solve; the flag is inline HTML on the receipt.
tech_stack: Composer 2.7 for a single JSON helper
labs.inspired_by: Business-logic classic; abstracted from countless HackerOne 'price tampering' reports 2016-2023, e.g. the well-known 'change price to 0.01' pattern documented in OWASP Business Logic Testing

labs.title: Negative Quantity Credit
labs.description: An Express cart endpoint accepts POST /cart/add with {sku, qty} and computes line_total = qty * unit_price. qty is parsed with Number() and never checked for >0. A negative qty pushes the cart subtotal below zero; the checkout endpoint issues store credit equal to abs(subtotal) when subtotal < 0. The student learns that 'validation' means both type and range, and that arithmetic on user input needs positive-value assertions on every path.
labs.objective: End a checkout with store_credit_cents >= 100000 on your account, then buy the Diamond Item (SKU=diamond, $50) using only that credit. Loading /orders/{id} for that order returns the flag.
labs.flag_hint: GET /orders/{id} returns the flag when order.item_sku='diamond' AND order.paid_with='store_credit' AND order.status='paid'. Flag text lives in /flag.txt inside the container and is embedded in the JSON response by the order handler when the predicate holds.
skills_taught: store credit as an attack surface
reading Express route handlers for missing guards
labs.inspired_by: Shopify negative-quantity refund pattern (public HackerOne report #326  and similar), abstracted to a minimal cart app

labs.title: Skip the Payment Step
labs.description: A Django checkout walks users through /checkout/cart -> /checkout/address -> /checkout/pay -> /checkout/complete. Each step sets a boolean on the session, but /checkout/complete only checks address_set, not payment_confirmed. Posting directly to /checkout/complete after the address step finalizes an order with state='paid' and payment_id=NULL. The lab teaches state-machine thinking and the value of a single server-side authoritative status field.
labs.objective: Place an order for the Prem-Access ticket (SKU=prem-ticket, $200) with payment_confirmed=False but order.status='paid'. Then GET /me/tickets/{ticket_id} to receive the flag.
labs.flag_hint: GET /me/tickets/{id} returns the flag from /flag.txt when Ticket.order.status='paid' AND Ticket.order.payment_id IS NULL. No separate solve endpoint; the ticket detail view carries the flag when the predicate matches.
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'Insufficient workflow validation' apprentice lab; also the 2022 HackerOne report family on ecommerce checkouts that finalize on address confirmation

labs.title: Promo Code Length Oracle
labs.description: The site rejects invalid promo codes with {"error":"invalid"} and accepts valid ones with {"error":"already used by another account"} (longer body). The student writes a wordlist enumerator that binary-searches by Content-Length. The target code SUMMER2026-VIP unlocks a 99% discount on any item. This is the friendliest possible intro to response-based oracles and rate-limit-free brute forcing; every step is observable in Burp's Comparer.
labs.objective: Discover the valid promo code by content-length differential, apply it to the Founders Pass ($5000), and complete the order. GET /orders/{id} returns the flag when order.total_cents <= 5000 (i.e. >=99% discount) AND coupon_code matches the seeded valid code.
labs.flag_hint: GET /orders/{id} returns the flag; the handler reads /flag.txt when order.discount_pct >= 99 AND order.coupon_code = (the seeded code, which the checker.sh in /opt/checker also validates on demand for the grader).
labs.inspired_by: Uber promo-code enumeration disclosed 2016 (bevans, HackerOne); refreshed pattern seen repeatedly through 2023

labs.title: Coupon Double-Apply Race
labs.description: A single-use coupon (SAVE90, 90% off any item) is enforced via 'SELECT used FROM coupons ... FOR UPDATE' but on a table with no unique constraint on (coupon_id, order_id) and the code path forgets the FOR UPDATE on the read path in the /apply endpoint; instead it does SELECT then UPDATE in two queries under READ COMMITTED. Two parallel POST /cart/apply-coupon requests both see used=false, both write used=true, both stack their -90% into the same cart. Result: total goes negative; store credits the difference.
labs.objective: Apply SAVE90 twice to the same cart holding the Studio Bundle ($1000) so that the resulting order total_cents < 0 and store_credit issued > 0. Then load /me/credit to receive the flag.
labs.flag_hint: GET /me/credit returns the flag from /flag.txt when store_credit_cents > 0 for the requesting user. A background checker.sh in /opt/checker/verify.sh also inspects orders.applied_coupons for two rows with the same coupon_id and can be run for graded validation.
skills_taught: parallel HTTP with turbo-intruder or Go goroutines
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'Limit overrun with parallel requests' practitioner lab; the coupon variant appears in dozens of 2022-2024 HackerOne reports

labs.title: Currency Confusion Refund
labs.description: A payments service stores balances as (amount_minor, currency) but the refund handler dereferences the transaction row and issues a refund of amount_minor to the requesting user's default wallet without re-checking currency. Purchase $6 worth of IDR credit (100000 IDR minor units), then request refund; the refund handler credits 100000 minor units to your USD wallet -> $1000. Teaches that money is always (amount, currency) and never just amount.
labs.objective: Grow your USD wallet balance to at least $1000 (100000 cents) via the currency-confusion refund path without any deposit, then GET /wallet/usd/proof to receive the flag.
labs.flag_hint: GET /wallet/usd/proof returns the flag when usd_wallet.balance_cents >= 100000 AND total_usd_deposited == 0. Flag lives at /flag inside the container. checker.sh in /opt/checker cross-checks against ledger for offline grading.
labs.inspired_by: Revolut $20M currency-conversion refund incident (2022, publicly reported); pattern also documented in the 2023 'money currency confusion' talk at OWASP Global AppSec

labs.title: Fractional-Cent Truncation Bank
labs.description: A Spring Boot banking demo uses BigDecimal internally but truncates to two decimal places with setScale(2, RoundingMode.FLOOR) on the sender side and RoundingMode.HALF_UP on the receiver side. Transferring $0.005 leaves 0.005 on the receiver (rounds to $0.01) but debits $0.00 from the sender. A student writes a script that transfers 0.005 a few thousand times to grow a target account by real money out of thin air. Also teaches the classic 'salami slicing' fraud from Office Space / SuperMan 3.
labs.objective: Grow account BANK-VAULT-001 (initial balance $0.00) to >= $10000.00 using only your own account, without ever making a deposit. Then GET /vault/audit which returns the flag when target.balance >= 1000000 minor units.
labs.flag_hint: GET /vault/audit returns the flag when account.balance_minor >= 1000000 AND total_external_deposits == 0. Flag file mounted at /flag; checker.sh in /opt/checker verifies balance and audit trail.
labs.inspired_by: Classic salami-slicing / rounding-error fraud; refreshed by the 2022 crypto exchange 'penny rounding' abuse reports on immunefi.com

labs.title: Free Trial Limit Overrun
labs.description: A SaaS grants one 14-day trial per account. POST /trial/start does 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM trials WHERE user_id=?' then 'INSERT INTO trials ...' with no unique index and no serializable transaction. Firing five simultaneous /trial/start requests all pass count=0 and all insert. This lab emphasizes real single-endpoint TOCTOU with parallel requests, tests the student's ability to see the count-then-insert antipattern anywhere it appears (referrals, credits, invitations, free tiers).
labs.objective: Create at least 5 concurrently-active trial rows on your account (visible via GET /me/trials), then GET /me/perks which returns the flag when trial_count > 1.
labs.flag_hint: GET /me/perks returns the flag; the handler reads /flag.txt when SELECT COUNT(*) FROM trials WHERE user_id=? AND active=true is >= 2. checker.sh in /opt/checker uses the same query for offline grading.
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'Limit overrun race conditions' practitioner; pattern seen in the 2023 Robinhood trial-account report family

labs.title: Coupon Stacking Order-Of-Ops
labs.description: A store supports three coupon types: percent-off (PCT20), free-shipping (SHIP0), and BOGO (BUY1GET1). Each coupon validator only checks that it is not stacked with 'another of the same type'. The apply endpoint runs coupons in the order the user posts them, and the discount math is percent-then-BOGO-then-shipping. Applying PCT20 -> BOGO -> PCT20 (renamed via header trick) applies the percent twice; adding SHIP0 and a rebate coupon (REBATE10 that pays $10) drives total < 0. There is no race; this is a pure logic puzzle about combinator design.
labs.objective: Complete a checkout for the Deluxe Kit (SKU=deluxe, $80) with order.total_cents < 0. Then GET /orders/{id}/refund which returns the flag when refund_cents > order.gross_cents.
labs.flag_hint: GET /orders/{id}/refund returns the flag from /flag.txt when refund_cents > 0 AND order.total_cents < 0. checker.sh verifies applied_coupons array has >=3 entries.
labs.inspired_by: Shopify coupon stacking public disclosures (2020-2023) and PortSwigger 'Excessive trust in client-side controls' lab

labs.title: Self-Referral Bonus Farm
labs.description: The signup flow gives $10 to referrer and $10 to referee. Referral eligibility check normalizes emails by lowercasing but does not strip dots (gmail-style) nor +tag suffixes, and IP dedupe is off. The student registers alice@example.com, refers a.l.i.c.e+1@example.com, then +2, +3... Each referral pays out. Bonus: the payout row commits before referral row commits, so a crash / cancelled request still keeps the bonus (partial-failure logic).
labs.objective: Grow your primary account's wallet to >= $500 via referral bonuses only (no deposits, no product purchases). GET /wallet returns the flag when balance >= 50000 cents AND deposits_cents==0.
labs.flag_hint: GET /wallet returns the flag; server reads /flag.txt when balance_cents >= 50000 AND deposits_cents == 0. checker.sh verifies referred_user_emails share the same normalized base.
tech_stack: Redis 7 for rate-limits (intentionally scoped by email string)
labs.inspired_by: Robinhood / Airbnb / DoorDash referral abuse writeups 2020-2024; the '+tag bypass' pattern appears in over 30 disclosed HackerOne reports

labs.title: Add-To-Cart During Checkout
labs.description: A Laravel checkout snapshots cart.total_cents at /checkout/start (creates a checkout_session row) but re-reads cart.items at /checkout/complete when the order rows are inserted. The window between /checkout/start and /checkout/complete is unguarded. Add a $2 candy to the cart, hit /checkout/start with total=200, then race POST /cart/add with SKU=diamond ($5000), then POST /checkout/complete. The order ships the diamond and charges $2. Multi-endpoint state confusion, no fancy HTTP required.
labs.objective: Ship an order that contains the Diamond Ring (SKU=diamond, $5000) with total_cents_paid <= 500. GET /orders/{id}/summary returns the flag when the summary row has diamond in items and paid <= 500 cents.
labs.flag_hint: GET /orders/{id}/summary returns the flag from /flag.txt when items contains diamond AND paid_cents <= 500. checker.sh performs the same check.
skills_taught: designing checkout as an atomic transaction
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'Multi-endpoint race conditions' lab and multiple 2022 HackerOne 'add-to-cart after order review' reports

labs.title: Subscription Downgrade Refund Loop
labs.description: A monthly subscription refunds a prorated amount on downgrade. Because the last-upgrade timestamp is not stored, the refund is computed against days-remaining-in-current-period from the CURRENT date. Upgrade to Premium ($30/mo) on day 1, downgrade to Free on day 2 -> refund is 28/30 * $30 = $28. Charge again on day 3 for $30, downgrade day 4 -> another $28. Net: pay $60, receive $56 twice plus keep Premium features because the deactivation is queued and runs end-of-billing-period.
labs.objective: Accumulate account credit of at least $100 without any external top-up, and keep premium_active=true continuously for >= 24 sim-hours (docker time is accelerated 1min = 1 day via a /time/skip debug endpoint). GET /premium/proof returns the flag when both conditions hold.
labs.flag_hint: GET /premium/proof returns the flag when credit_cents >= 10000 AND premium_active_last_24sim_hours == true. checker.sh replays the ledger for verification.
tech_stack: Hangfire 1.8 for the queued deactivation job
labs.inspired_by: 2023 subscription-abuse writeup pattern on immunefi (SaaS billing); PortSwigger 'Flawed subscription lifecycle' concept

labs.title: One-Time Invite Code Race
labs.description: A closed-beta signup takes a one-time invite code. The code row is marked used inside the same transaction as user creation, but the /signup handler validates the code in a separate 'preflight' request called by the frontend before /signup POST; there is a 300ms gap. Two parallel /signup POSTs with the same code both pass preflight and both create users. Bonus: one of the created accounts inherits inviter_is_admin=true because the second insert also sets 'permissions' from the invite payload.
labs.objective: Create two active users with the invite code INV-BETA-042 such that one is a normal user and one has role=admin. Login as the admin user and GET /admin/panel to receive the flag.
labs.flag_hint: GET /admin/panel returns the flag when the requesting session has role=admin. The role column is populated by the vulnerable signup path. checker.sh verifies two users exist with the same invite_code_id.
skills_taught: single-use token protection with atomic UPDATE ... WHERE used=false
labs.inspired_by: Clubhouse / early-access invite reuse writeups (2021); pattern refreshed in the 2024 HackerOne 'closed beta signup race' family

labs.title: Password Reset Token Confusion
labs.description: The Rails password reset flow issues a JWT token bound to email but the /reset/confirm endpoint looks up the user by the token's sub claim (numeric user id) rather than re-verifying the email. Two accounts share an old email history: admin@corp.local currently uses admin@corp.local, and the attacker signs up new-user@corp.local then updates its email to admin@corp.local (previous-email history retained). Requesting reset for admin@corp.local dispatches the token to new-user@corp.local via the email-history lookup, which is delivered to a mailhog container the student can browse.
labs.objective: Take over the admin account by exploiting the email-history reset flow. Log in as admin and GET /admin/flag which returns the flag when session.user.email='admin@corp.local' AND session.user.role='admin'.
labs.flag_hint: GET /admin/flag returns the flag from /flag.txt when the authenticated user is the seeded admin. Student reads the reset email in the bundled mailhog UI at :8025.
skills_taught: user lookup by id vs. by verified email
labs.inspired_by: Uber account takeover via email-alias reset (public writeup 2019 by Anand Prakash); pattern still surfaces regularly through 2024

labs.title: Approve-Then-Cancel Transfer Race
labs.description: A B2B money transfer workflow is Draft -> PendingApproval -> Approved -> Executed, with a cancel button available in any state except Executed. The Approve handler debits sender and enqueues an async Execute job; the Cancel handler refunds sender if state != Executed. Racing Approve and Cancel: state becomes Approved AND Cancel refunds sender AND the Execute job still runs (it re-reads state=Approved after the cancel wrote state=Cancelled but before it committed, due to READ COMMITTED). Net: sender is refunded AND receiver still gets money.
labs.objective: Cause the total balance across sender+receiver to exceed the initial total by at least $500 (i.e. print money). GET /audit/proof returns the flag when SUM(balances) > initial_total by >= 50000 cents.
labs.flag_hint: GET /audit/proof returns the flag from /flag.txt when the sum-of-balances invariant is broken by >= 50000 cents. checker.sh replays journal entries and inspects final state.
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'Multi-endpoint race conditions' expert lab and the 2023 Immunefi 'approve+cancel' DAO treasury family

labs.title: JWT Refresh Token Race
labs.description: The refresh endpoint reads the refresh_token row, mints a new access_token derived from user.roles at that instant, then marks refresh_token used, all in three non-atomic calls. Two parallel POST /auth/refresh with the same refresh_token both pass the used=false check. In parallel, the attacker POSTs /admin/promote-me which only sometimes succeeds (a small backdoor for the challenge that requires role=beta) but is a red herring; the real trick is that a race window exists between two /auth/refresh calls where the user's roles are updated by a background job (seeded) that grants role=admin for 200ms before revoking. The student's parallel refresh captures a token in that window that persists after revocation.
labs.objective: Obtain an access_token where JWT claim roles contains 'admin'. Use it against GET /admin/flag which reads and returns /flag.txt when the presented JWT is valid and roles contains 'admin'.
labs.flag_hint: GET /admin/flag validates JWT signature (HS256, key mounted from /run/secrets/jwt) and returns /flag.txt when claims.roles contains 'admin'. checker.sh inspects a captured token if provided.
skills_taught: capturing tokens minted in a race window
labs.inspired_by: OAuth2 refresh-token rotation TOCTOU family, publicly reported against several IdPs 2022-2024

labs.title: Single-Packet Attack: Bank Transfer
labs.description: A high-latency bank service (500ms artificial DB delay on balance read, 5ms on write) makes classic parallel HTTP unreliable. Real exploitation requires HTTP/2 last-byte synchronization (single-packet attack, James Kettle 2023) to arrive at the server within the same 1ms window and race the balance check. The student starts a $100 transfer from a $50 wallet three times; only single-packet timing succeeds. The lab documents connection warming (send one dummy request first) and how to observe race success via a debug counter at /debug/races-passed.
labs.objective: Drain the victim wallet VICTIM-01 (initial $50) below -$100 by executing at least three concurrent $100 transfers to your attacker wallet. GET /audit/victim returns the flag when victim.balance_cents <= -10000.
labs.flag_hint: GET /audit/victim returns the flag from /flag.txt when VICTIM-01.balance_cents <= -10000. Requires HTTP/2 to the challenge origin at https://race.local. checker.sh replays the ledger for grading.
skills_taught: artificial latency and race window sizing
tech_stack: Postgres 16 (READ COMMITTED, deliberate 500ms sleep in balance read)
nginx 1.27 as HTTP/2 front-end with keep-alive
labs.inspired_by: James Kettle 'Smashing the state machine' (PortSwigger 2023) - single-packet attack research

labs.title: Marketplace Single-Item Race
labs.description: A Rails marketplace lists a unique second-hand collectible (stock=1). The purchase flow does SELECT stock, INSERT order, UPDATE stock=stock-1 under READ COMMITTED with no row lock. Two buyer accounts (student controls both) hit /buy in parallel; both orders succeed, stock goes to -1, and both buyers are shown the item as owned. Ownership is reflected in /items/{id} which lists the current owner. Bonus: the seller's ledger is credited twice, letting the student verify the double-spend from three sides (both buyers + seller).
labs.objective: Get both attacker accounts (buyer-a and buyer-b) listed as owners of item-rare-001 in /items/rare-001/owners, then GET /items/rare-001/owners which returns the flag when the owners array length >= 2.
labs.flag_hint: GET /items/rare-001/owners returns the flag when JSON owners.length >= 2. checker.sh verifies orders table has >=2 rows with item_id=rare-001 and stock < 0.
tech_stack: Postgres 16 (READ COMMITTED, no FOR UPDATE, no unique constraint)
labs.inspired_by: eBay-style limited-drop race writeups; StockX / Supreme bot patterns 2020-2024

labs.title: Booking Slot Double-Book
labs.description: A Django appointment system reserves slots by inserting into a bookings table with only an application-level 'if not exists' check across (slot_id, day). Django's default REPEATABLE READ on Postgres is not used; the manage command sets ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED intentionally. Two parallel POST /book with slot=vip-consult&day=2026-09-05 both insert. The VIP slot handler grants elevated permissions to whoever holds the booking; both accounts get them, but the second insert triggers a hidden 'audit override' path used only when duplicate bookings exist, exposing an internal admin dashboard endpoint.
labs.objective: Book the VIP slot (slot_id=vip-consult) for day 2026-09-05 with two distinct user accounts simultaneously. Then GET /admin/audit-override which returns the flag when audit_override_triggered=true.
labs.flag_hint: GET /admin/audit-override returns the flag from /flag.txt when audit_override_triggered=true AND the requesting user holds a VIP booking. checker.sh verifies duplicate bookings.
labs.inspired_by: OpenTable / Airbnb / Calendly booking race patterns 2022-2024 (multiple HackerOne reports)

labs.title: KYC Verification Hijack
labs.description: A Laravel fintech verifies identity documents through a two-step flow: POST /kyc/upload accepts a driver's license PDF and returns a doc_id; POST /kyc/bind {doc_id, account_id} attaches it to an account. /kyc/bind trusts account_id from the body and does not verify the caller owns account_id. Attacker uploads their own genuine documents, then binds them to admin@corp.local's account. Admin was previously blocked because kyc_verified=false; the block lifts, exposing /admin/panel. Pure logic (BOLA family) but with just enough plumbing (MinIO, PDF magic bytes check) to feel real.
labs.objective: Cause admin@corp.local's account to have kyc_verified=true using documents you uploaded, then log in as the seeded admin (session_hijack helper provided) and GET /admin/panel which returns the flag.
labs.flag_hint: GET /admin/panel returns the flag from /flag.txt when the authenticated user has kyc_verified=true AND role=admin. checker.sh inspects kyc_bindings and admin_user state.
labs.inspired_by: Multiple 2023 fintech HackerOne KYC-bypass reports (abstracted); pattern also present in the 2024 Coinbase Institutional bug-bounty program summary

labs.title: Connection-Warmed OTP Reuse
labs.description: A vault-unlock flow requires a 6-digit OTP delivered via a webhook the student can read. The OTP is single-use (marked used inside the /vault/unlock handler) but the check-then-use gap is <5ms because both operations hit Redis rather than Postgres. Parallel HTTP hits the front-end nginx which serializes requests within a single TCP connection; the trick is (a) HTTP/2 multiplexing and (b) connection warming so both streams arrive at the app in the same event loop tick. Success unlocks the vault which serves /flag.txt as JSON.
labs.objective: Unlock the vault twice with the same OTP within a 5-second window. GET /vault/contents returns the flag from /flag.txt when unlock_count >= 2 AND unique_otps_used == 1.
labs.flag_hint: GET /vault/contents returns the flag from /flag.txt when unlock_count >= 2 with a single distinct OTP in the audit table. checker.sh inspects the audit table.
skills_taught: connection warming with a dummy request
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'connection warming' technique (Kettle 2023); OTP reuse pattern seen in several fintech disclosures 2023-2024

labs.title: HTTP/2 Downgrade Tunneling Race
labs.description: A haproxy 2.9 front-end speaks HTTP/2 to clients and HTTP/1.1 to a Go origin. The origin does not enforce Content-Length vs. Transfer-Encoding strictly, and haproxy's h2-to-h1 translation with :authority overrides opens a request-smuggling primitive (CVE-2023-25725 / CVE-2023-45539 class). The student smuggles a coupon-application request that piggybacks in the same TCP session as the victim's checkout, bypassing per-connection rate limits and racing the coupon-single-use guard from inside the same connection. Combined with a single-packet timing trick, the student redeems a $500 coupon three times.
labs.objective: Redeem coupon FOUNDERS-500 three times against your account using an HTTP/2 downgrade tunneling primitive. GET /wallet/statement returns the flag when applied_founders_500_count >= 3.
labs.flag_hint: GET /wallet/statement returns the flag from /flag.txt when applied_founders_500_count >= 3 for the requesting user. checker.sh verifies the coupon audit table.
skills_taught: combining smuggling with single-packet race timing
tech_stack: haproxy 2.9 (HTTP/2 frontend, HTTP/1.1 backend, strict-mode intentionally disabled)
nginx 1.27 as the second-hop origin sidecar
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'HTTP/2: The sequel is always worse' (Kettle 2021); CVE-2023-25725 (haproxy header smuggling); the 2024 h2-tunneling races talk at DEF CON AppSec Village

labs.title: Distributed Lock Bypass Across Microservices
labs.description: A cart-service and a coupon-service coordinate via a Redlock (redlock-py) on a shared Redis. The lock key is derived from cart_id but coupon-service resolves cart_id from a JWT claim, and cart-service also accepts a header X-Debug-Cart-Id that supersedes the JWT (leftover from debugging). By presenting two cart_ids (one in JWT, one in header) across the two services, the student holds a lock on cart-A while mutating cart-B, defeating mutual exclusion. Layered on top is a real race: SAVE100 (100% off) coupon single-use, applied to cart-B while cart-A holds the lock, yielding a $0 order for the Diamond Bundle ($10000).
labs.objective: Ship an order for the Diamond Bundle (SKU=diamond-bundle, $10000) with paid_cents=0 using SAVE100. GET /orders/{id}/receipt returns the flag when the predicate matches.
labs.flag_hint: GET /orders/{id}/receipt returns the flag from /flag.txt when items contains diamond-bundle AND paid_cents==0 AND coupon_code='SAVE100'. checker.sh verifies orders and audit tables across both services.
skills_taught: chaining logic (header override) with concurrency (coupon race)
labs.inspired_by: Martin Kleppmann's 'How to do distributed locking' critique of Redlock (2016); pattern also documented in the 2023 Grab.com engineering post on coupon abuse

labs.title: Chained: Currency + Race + Marketplace Takeover
labs.description: Capstone chain across three vulnerabilities. Step 1: promo-code enumeration by response-length differential discovers coupon INTERNAL-DEBUG-99 (99% off, unlimited use, admin-marker true). Step 2: apply the coupon twice via single-packet HTTP/2 race to a checkout that stacks it against itself, driving order.total_cents negative, which triggers a store-credit issuance in USD. Step 3: use the USD credit in a currency-confusion refund path to convert it into IDR at 1:1 minor units, then refund the IDR into an admin-owned wallet (accessible because the coupon marked the session as admin-tagged, exposing /admin/refund which does not check destination ownership). Result: admin wallet drained AND attacker credit remains. Final flag served only after admin_wallet.balance == 0 AND attacker.usd_credit > 0.
labs.objective: Simultaneously bring ADMIN-WALLET.balance to 0 AND grow your ATTACKER-WALLET usd_credit to >= $10000, using the full chain above. GET /grader/final returns the flag when both invariants hold.
labs.flag_hint: GET /grader/final returns the flag from /flag.txt when ADMIN-WALLET.balance_cents==0 AND ATTACKER-WALLET.usd_credit_cents >= 1000000. checker.sh in /opt/checker/verify.sh performs the same joint check and prints a per-stage progress table for partial credit.
skills_taught: admin path discovery via session tagging
tech_stack: nginx 1.27 with HTTP/2 termination + h2c upstream
labs.inspired_by: Composite of James Kettle 2023 single-packet research, the 2022 Revolut currency-conversion incident, and the 2024 Coinbase 'chained business-logic' bug-bounty writeup family

labs.title: Classic XXE: Reading /etc/passwd via External Entity
labs.description: A minimalist stock-quote lookup service accepts an XML payload describing which ticker symbols to query. The backend parses the payload with libxml2 in its stock default configuration (LIBXML_NOENT | LIBXML_DTDLOAD enabled) and echoes the resolved <symbol> content back to the user. Because the parser resolves external entities without restriction, a crafted DOCTYPE with a file:// system identifier lets the attacker replace the ticker text with the contents of any file readable by the web process.
labs.objective: Submit an XML payload to POST /api/quote that causes the response to include the contents of /flag.txt (mode 0644, owned by root, mounted into the container at build time).
labs.flag_hint: The flag is a static file at /flag.txt inside the container in the format flag{apprentice-classic-xxe-<random-hex>}; the user simply copies the string out of the HTTP response body once they get file read working.
skills_taught: reading source of an HTTP response for exfil
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger Web Security Academy 'Exploiting XXE using external entities to retrieve files' plus HackerOne report #1189367 (SendGrid XXE, 2022 disclosure)

labs.title: XPath Injection: Authentication Bypass in an XML User Store
labs.description: A legacy intranet SSO shim stores its user database as an XML file on disk and authenticates by building an XPath expression via naive string concatenation: //user[username/text()='$u' and password/text()='$p']. There is no prepared-statement equivalent in the code path and no input validation. Classic OR-tautology payloads collapse the predicate and return the first <user> node, which the app treats as a successful login.
labs.objective: Log in as the user 'administrator' without knowing the password by submitting a crafted username or password to POST /login, then visit /admin to retrieve the flag rendered in the dashboard.
labs.flag_hint: The /admin page reads /var/lib/app/flag.txt and echoes it inside a <div id='flag'> element only when the session cookie carries role=administrator; the flag format is flag{apprentice-xpath-bypass-<uuid>}.
skills_taught: the difference between XPath and SQL injection
labs.inspired_by: OWASP XPath Injection cheat sheet reference implementation and the 2023 Bugcrowd 'Bypassing authentication via XPath injection in a vendor portal' blog write-up

labs.title: Billion Laughs: Denial of Service via Recursive Entity Expansion
labs.description: A configuration-import endpoint on an internal monitoring dashboard accepts XML uploads and parses them synchronously in the request thread with Java's default DocumentBuilderFactory (secure processing disabled, no entity expansion limit). The classic lol1..lol9 nested entity payload expands to a billion 'lol' tokens, consuming multiple gigabytes of heap and stalling the JVM long enough for the liveness probe to reap the pod.
labs.objective: Submit a payload to POST /admin/import that causes the /healthz endpoint on port 8080 to return non-200 (or connection refused) for at least 10 consecutive seconds; the platform's checker polls /healthz once per second.
labs.flag_hint: A sidecar container watches /healthz; once 10 consecutive failures are recorded within 30 seconds it writes /shared/flag.txt (bind-mounted read-only into the app container at /flag.txt) and the user retrieves it via GET /flag after the app recovers. Format: flag{apprentice-billion-laughs-<hex>}.
tech_stack: Docker with --memory=1g cap so exhaustion is reachable
labs.inspired_by: CVE-2003-1564 (original billion laughs) modernised, and the 2024 Snyk report on Spring Boot deployments still shipping DocumentBuilderFactory without secure-processing

labs.title: XXE via SVG Avatar Upload
labs.description: A social-profile microservice lets users upload an SVG avatar which the server rasterises to PNG using librsvg through a Node.js binding. Before rasterisation the SVG is parsed with libxmljs2 with default options that permit external entities. Because SVG is XML, an SVG file containing a DOCTYPE with a SYSTEM entity is dereferenced during parsing; the resolved text ends up baked into a <text> element in the rendered PNG.
labs.objective: Upload an SVG file to POST /profile/avatar such that the resulting rendered avatar image (returned at GET /profile/avatar/<id>.png) visibly contains the first line of /etc/hostname AND the contents of /flag.txt.
labs.flag_hint: The flag lives at /flag.txt (readable by node user) in format flag{apprentice-svg-xxe-<hex>}; the user OCRs or eyeballs it from the rendered avatar PNG. A hint page at /docs shows a working SVG skeleton.
skills_taught: SVG is XML and inherits every XML parser flaw
using rendered text nodes as an exfil channel
labs.inspired_by: HackerOne #1109311 (avatar SVG XXE against Grafana Cloud, disclosed 2022) and Assetnote's 2023 'SVG upload XXE — still finding it' research

labs.title: XXE in an RSS/Atom Aggregator
labs.description: A tiny 'news reader' service accepts a URL, fetches the feed, parses it with Python's xml.etree.ElementTree, and displays titles in the dashboard. The developer swapped defusedxml for xml.etree at some point 'because it was faster' but did not disable external entities in the fallback path. Any RSS/Atom feed the attacker hosts (or supplies as a data: URL) can therefore be crafted with a DOCTYPE that reads local files.
labs.objective: Cause the /dashboard page to render the contents of /flag.txt in the position where the first feed item's <title> normally appears; you may host the malicious feed inside the lab network at http://attacker:9000/ (a pre-provisioned nginx container that serves whatever you PUT to it).
labs.flag_hint: Flag is a static file /flag.txt in format flag{apprentice-rss-xxe-<hex>}. The dashboard's HTML source is the exfil channel; a solve script at /solve accepts a POST containing the flag and returns 200 when correct, but is not required.
skills_taught: hosting attacker-controlled XML on the lab network
RSS/Atom as an XML attack surface
tech_stack: docker-compose 2.29 with an 'attacker' nginx 1.27 sidecar on port 9000
labs.inspired_by: Snyk 2022 advisory on xml.etree footguns and the CVE-2022-40982-adjacent 'feed reader XXE' write-ups on r/netsec

labs.title: Blind XXE with Out-of-Band Exfiltration via Parameter Entities
labs.description: A B2B invoice-processing API accepts XML documents but strips the response body, returning only {"status":"queued"}. The parser (Xerces via Spring's Jaxb2Marshaller) allows external DTD loading and parameter entities. The attacker must host a malicious DTD on the lab's OOB host that defines a parameter entity referencing a local file and a second parameter entity that concatenates the file contents into an HTTP callback URL, exfiltrating the data across the wire.
labs.objective: Exfiltrate the entire contents of /opt/app/config/secret.properties to http://attacker:9000/log?data=<...> where 'attacker' is a pre-provisioned collector container that stores every request path to /var/log/oob/requests.log.
labs.flag_hint: The collector container exposes GET /collected which returns the concatenated query strings it has received. The user must reassemble the URL-encoded file contents; the flag is a line inside secret.properties formatted as flag{practitioner-blind-xxe-oob-<hex>}.
tech_stack: docker-compose stack: app + attacker (nginx 1.27 + tiny Go collector on port 9000)
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'Blind XXE with out-of-band interaction via XML parameter entities', HackerOne #712065 style, and 2023 write-up on blind XXE in an invoicing SaaS by Assetnote

labs.title: Error-Based XXE: Folding File Contents Into an Error Message
labs.description: The same class of endpoint as the blind lab, but now the OOB host is firewalled off — only the app's own domain is reachable. However, verbose XML parse errors are returned to the client. By crafting a parameter entity that expands a file's contents into an invalid SYSTEM identifier ('file:///nonexistent/<file-content>'), the parser throws an IOException whose message contains the resolved path — and therefore the file's contents.
labs.objective: Retrieve the contents of /home/appuser/.aws/credentials by triggering an XML parser error at POST /api/xmlimport whose response body contains the full credential file, then submit the AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY value to POST /solve.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve with JSON {"secret":"<value>"} returns {"flag":"flag{practitioner-error-based-xxe-<hex>}"} on match, else 401. Credentials file mounted at build time.
skills_taught: constructing invalid SYSTEM URIs on purpose
why blind is not always blind
tech_stack: network policy blocking egress to non-app hosts (via iptables in an init container)
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'Exploiting blind XXE to retrieve data via error messages' and the 2022 GitLab CVE-2022-2185 error-oracle style pattern

labs.title: XXE via DOCX Upload in a Resume Parser
labs.description: A recruiter tool extracts text from uploaded resumes. DOCX files are ZIP containers holding several XML parts (word/document.xml, [Content_Types].xml, docProps/core.xml). The Python-docx-based parser reads word/document.xml with lxml without disabling entity resolution. Users unzip a benign .docx, inject a DOCTYPE with an external entity into word/document.xml, re-zip, and upload.
labs.objective: Upload a malicious .docx to POST /resume/upload so that the rendered candidate profile at GET /resume/<id> contains the contents of /flag.txt, which is only readable by the appuser account.
labs.flag_hint: /flag.txt at container root, mode 0400, owned by appuser. Format flag{practitioner-docx-xxe-<hex>}. The lab ships a helper docx-repack.py script in the README that automates the zip-edit-rezip cycle so users focus on the payload.
skills_taught: why 'we only accept .docx not .xml' is not a defence
labs.inspired_by: HackerOne #347139 (docx XXE on Semmle), the 2023 disclosure of XXE in a well-known ATS vendor by Assetnote, and CVE-2023-27524-adjacent recruiter-tool patterns

labs.title: XXE in a Legacy SOAP Endpoint
labs.description: An internal HR system exposes a SOAP endpoint (deployed with Apache CXF) that consumes employee records. The XML envelope is parsed with a StAX reader whose IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES property is left at its default (true in this version). Injecting an external entity into a SOAP body element causes the entity to be resolved and echoed into the SOAP response's response element.
labs.objective: Send a crafted SOAP request to POST /ws/employees that returns the contents of /etc/shadow (readable in this deliberately-misconfigured container) inside the <return> element of the response envelope.
labs.flag_hint: /etc/shadow contains a fake hash line for user 'flagbearer' whose 'password field' is the flag itself: flag{practitioner-soap-xxe-<hex>}. The user extracts it from the SOAP response body.
skills_taught: why SOAP is still everywhere in the enterprise
tech_stack: Docker: root-owned /etc/shadow with a synthetic entry
labs.inspired_by: CVE-2022-46364 (Apache CXF SSRF/XXE), MITRE ATT&CK T1190 examples, and 2023 write-up on SOAP XXE in a healthcare integration bus

labs.title: Blind Boolean-Based XPath Injection
labs.description: A password-reset lookup endpoint takes a username and returns HTTP 200 if it exists, 404 otherwise. Internally it evaluates //user[username/text()='<input>'] against an XML file containing dozens of users. The response body is identical for every 200, so there is no error/text oracle — but the status code is a perfect boolean. The attacker uses XPath's substring() and string-length() functions to extract the admin's password character-by-character.
labs.objective: Recover the full 'apitoken' element value of the user 'root' from the XML store (which never appears in any response body) and submit it to POST /solve.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve with {"token":"<value>"} returns the flag flag{practitioner-blind-xpath-<hex>} on match. The XML store is mounted read-only at /var/lib/app/users.xml so the writer of a solve script can sanity-check.
skills_taught: difference between XPath 1.0 and 2.0/3.1 attack surface
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger XPath injection labs, HackerOne #1046084 (blind XPath in an enterprise wiki, 2022), and OWASP Testing Guide OTG-INPVAL-010

labs.title: XSLT Injection: PHP's xsl:document Reading Local Files
labs.description: A reporting endpoint lets users upload a custom XSLT stylesheet to transform their sales data. The XSLTProcessor is instantiated with default settings and — critically — without calling setSecurityPrefs() to forbid document(), read/write file, and script. Attackers upload a stylesheet using <xsl:value-of select="document('file:///flag.txt')"/> to fold arbitrary files into the transformed output.
labs.objective: Upload a stylesheet at POST /report/transform whose HTML output contains the entire contents of /flag.txt.
labs.flag_hint: /flag.txt in the container root; format flag{practitioner-xslt-php-xsl-doc-<hex>}. The transformed output is rendered directly at GET /report/<id>.
skills_taught: the document() function as a file-read primitive
PHP XSLTProcessor::setSecurityPrefs and why it is off by default
how to smuggle payloads into innocuous-looking stylesheets
labs.inspired_by: Balgan's classic XSLT-in-PHP research, the 2023 HackerOne report on a marketing-analytics vendor allowing user XSLT uploads, and Snyk advisory SNYK-PHP-EXT-XSL-2024

labs.title: SSRF and Internal Port-Scanning via XXE DTD Retrieval
labs.description: A newsroom CMS validates uploaded XML against a DTD referenced by an http:// SYSTEM identifier. The parser (lxml with load_dtd=True and no_network=False) blindly fetches whatever URL is supplied. The attacker weaponises the fetch to probe internal-only services on 10.0.0.0/8, distinguishing open/closed/filtered ports by response-time and by the resulting parse-error message.
labs.objective: Enumerate which of ports 80, 3306, 6379, 8500 are listening on the internal host 'internal-services.lab' (a sidecar with only a few of those actually up), then submit the sorted CSV of open ports to POST /solve.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve {"open":"80,6379"} returns flag{practitioner-xxe-ssrf-portscan-<hex>} on match. The sidecar deliberately runs only a subset chosen randomly at container start and written to /shared/expected.txt.
skills_taught: distinguishing port states from parser behaviour
internal reconnaissance from a public endpoint
why external DTD loading is dangerous even without file:// entities
tech_stack: docker-compose network with 'internal-services' sidecar running randomised set of {nginx, redis, mysql, consul}
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'Exploiting XXE to perform SSRF attacks', HackerOne #158434 (Uber SSRF via XXE), and the 2024 disclosure of DTD-based SSRF in a major CI/CD product

labs.title: XInclude When DOCTYPE is Blocked
labs.description: The security team of a policy-engine service disabled DOCTYPE declarations at the parser level, believing they had killed XXE. But the parser (Java's Woodstox with XInclude processing turned on) still honours <xi:include>. Because XInclude is triggered by element markup rather than a DOCTYPE, it slips right past the DOCTYPE-only filter and provides a file-read primitive.
labs.objective: Submit a policy document to POST /policy/validate that uses xi:include to embed /var/lib/policy/master.key into the validation response, then paste the key value into POST /solve.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve returns flag{practitioner-xinclude-<hex>} when the correct 64-hex-char master key is submitted; the key is generated on container start and only readable by the appuser account.
skills_taught: why filter ladders that block only DOCTYPE fail
adversarial testing of 'we blocked XXE' claims
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'Exploiting XInclude to retrieve files', and the 2023 disclosure by Detectify of an XInclude bypass in a well-known policy-as-code product

labs.title: XXE via XLSX SharedStrings
labs.description: A spreadsheet ingestion pipeline (a SaaS import step) parses the shared-strings XML part of uploaded XLSX files with SheetJS's built-in XML reader configured to expand external entities. Because XLSX is a ZIP of XML parts, exactly the same DOCTYPE injection that works against DOCX works here — but the vulnerable part is xl/sharedStrings.xml, and the exfil channel is the rendered cell value in the imported preview.
labs.objective: Upload an XLSX to POST /import/xlsx such that the preview at GET /import/<id>/preview shows the contents of /flag.txt in cell A1.
labs.flag_hint: /flag.txt is world-readable, format flag{practitioner-xlsx-xxe-<hex>}. Users can build the malicious XLSX with the ship-with-repo scripts/repack-xlsx.sh helper.
skills_taught: shared strings table as an attack surface
labs.inspired_by: Follina/Microsoft Office ZIP-XML mindset (2022), Assetnote 2024 'XXE in enterprise import pipelines' post, and HackerOne #1476780 on an XLSX XXE in a data-analytics vendor

labs.title: Bypassing a WAF's XXE Filter with UTF-16 Encoding
labs.description: A WAF fronts the app and rejects any request body containing the ASCII strings '<!ENTITY', 'SYSTEM', 'DOCTYPE', or 'file:'. The XML parser downstream, however, honours the encoding declared in the XML prolog. Serialising the malicious document in UTF-16LE (with BOM) produces bytes that do not contain those ASCII substrings — the WAF passes them through, and the parser happily decodes them. A second layer uses hex-encoded parameter entities to obscure the file URI once inside the parser.
labs.objective: Retrieve /var/lib/app/private.pem through POST /api/xml and submit the SHA-256 of the file to POST /solve.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve {"sha256":"<hex>"} returns flag{expert-utf16-xxe-<hex>}. private.pem is generated at container start and never leaves the file system otherwise.
skills_taught: reading the WAF ruleset in the docs to prove the bypass class
tech_stack: ModSecurity 3.0 with a custom XXE rule set in front (Nginx 1.27 as gateway)
labs.inspired_by: PortSwigger 'XXE via modified content type' variant, Trustwave SpiderLabs 2022 UTF-16 WAF bypass write-up, and CVE-2023-28879-adjacent parser-encoding mismatch bugs

labs.title: .NET XmlDocument XXE (Legacy Default Behavior)
labs.description: An older-style ASP.NET Core service uses System.Xml.XmlDocument to parse incoming SAML-lite metadata. Under .NET Framework 4.5.2+ defaults, XmlResolver on XmlDocument is null, but this codebase explicitly assigns a new XmlUrlResolver 'because we needed to load schemas'. That single line reintroduces the full XXE surface, and the SAML metadata parser echoes attributes back into the assertion response.
labs.objective: Read C:\inetpub\secrets\flag.txt (Windows container) via POST /saml/metadata and submit the string to POST /solve.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve returns flag{expert-dotnet-xmldocument-xxe-<hex>} when the file contents match. The flag file is mounted at C:\inetpub\secrets\flag.txt at build time.
skills_taught: XmlDocument vs XmlReader vs XDocument defaults
how one line (XmlResolver = new XmlUrlResolver()) reopens XXE
labs.inspired_by: MSRC advisory MSRC-2022-XmlDocument-guidance, HackerOne #1218988 (XXE in a .NET SAML consumer), and Rhino Security Labs 2023 'Still-exploitable XXE in .NET Framework apps'

labs.title: Java Xalan XSLT: RCE via Runtime.exec Extension
labs.description: A tax-return rendering microservice uses Apache Xalan-J to apply user-supplied XSLT stylesheets. Xalan's default extension mechanism allows Java class instantiation from XSLT via the xmlns:rt="http://xml.apache.org/xalan/java/java.lang.Runtime" namespace hack. A stylesheet can call Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...) and pipe the command output back into the transformed document.
labs.objective: Upload a stylesheet to POST /return/render that executes /read-flag.sh (a helper in the container that prints /flag.txt) and embeds the output in the rendered PDF preview at GET /return/<id>/preview.
labs.flag_hint: /flag.txt is chmod 0400 root; /read-flag.sh is a setuid wrapper. Format: flag{expert-xalan-xslt-rce-<hex>}. Users copy the flag out of the preview HTML.
skills_taught: XSLT as a code-execution primitive, not just data transformation
why 'the parser is sandboxed' is often untrue
chained extensions for command output capture
labs.inspired_by: OWASP XSLT Server Side Injection reference, the 2023 CVE-2023-49760 (adjacent Xalan-in-product) disclosure, and Vulhub's historic Xalan RCE demo

labs.title: Python lxml XXE Through a defusedxml Blind Spot
labs.description: The team wrapped every parser call with defusedxml.lxml.fromstring, believing they had solved XXE. However, one legacy code path uses lxml.etree.XMLParser(resolve_entities=False) but then reassembles the tree and re-serialises it, later feeding the serialised string into lxml.etree.fromstring with default arguments (entities resolved). The attacker crafts a payload where the exfil-inducing entity survives the round-trip because the intermediate step preserves the DOCTYPE textually.
labs.objective: Read /var/lib/app/kms.token via POST /pipeline/ingest and submit the value to POST /solve.
labs.flag_hint: POST /solve returns flag{expert-python-lxml-defusedxml-gap-<hex>} when the token matches. The token is generated per-container-start.
skills_taught: defusedxml is not a magic sticker
auditing every parse call, not just the top-level one
labs.inspired_by: PyCQA 2023 advisories on defusedxml misuse, HackerOne #1553894 (XXE in a Python analytics pipeline), and the 2024 'defusedxml is not enough' Snyk blog

labs.title: Ruby Nokogiri XXE in a Feed Import Path
labs.description: A Rails app imports OPML/feed bundles using Nokogiri::XML(io). Nokogiri disables network access and DTD loading by default in recent versions — but this code path explicitly passes Nokogiri::XML::ParseOptions::DTDLOAD | ::NOENT because a maintainer wanted 'compatibility with old feed formats'. Additionally, the same handler serialises the parsed doc back with to_xml before re-parsing it for indexing, giving a second parse point.
